text:
Over the past few months, a curiously coordinated alarm has been sounding from the upper echelons of Silicon Valley and Washington. Artificial intelligence, we are told, is on the brink of escaping human control. Left in the wrong hands, open-source models—software whose underlying weights can be downloaded, inspected and run on private hardware—supposedly pose a catastrophic threat to public safety, national security and critical infrastructure. The remedy, offered with suspicious speed, is always the same: licensing regimes, strict limits on who may run advanced models locally, and heavy penalties for anyone who steps outside the approved perimeter.

Before the public unwittingly accepts a new architecture of state-backed controls, it is worth asking one simple question. Who actually stands to lose if open-source artificial intelligence succeeds?

The most obvious answer is not the general public, nor even the national grid. It is the small circle of frontier laboratories—chief among them OpenAI and Anthropic—that have raised tens of billions of dollars on the promise of owning the defining technology of the century. Their business model rests on scarcity and rent. You do not own their software; you rent access to it through a metered cloud, on their servers, under their terms of service, subject to their moderation rules.

That model worked cleanly enough while frontier performance required vast corporate data centres. It began to wobble the moment free, open-weight models—many of them released by Chinese labs and independent research groups—started closing the gap. When a capable model can be downloaded once and run on a desktop workstation at a fraction of the cost, the commercial moat around closed, subscription-based AI narrows rapidly. Viewed in that light, the sudden urgency around "AI safety" looks less like a humanitarian awakening and more like a familiar piece of industrial lobbying: protectionism dressed up in the language of existential risk.

The same logic sits behind the increasingly theatrical warnings about "rogue AI". In the popular telling, we are supposed to imagine autonomous machines waking up and deciding to wage war on humanity. In reality, software does not have motives, grudges or political ambitions. When an automated system probes a network or disrupts a service, it is executing objectives prompted by human operators. Blaming the underlying code is rather like blaming the printing press for sedition, or a spanner for a burglary. The phrase "rogue AI" is useful precisely because it shifts attention away from human accountability and towards the idea that the tool itself is too dangerous for ordinary citizens to possess.

History offers a clear guide to how this sort of panic is converted into law. Public appetite for sweeping restrictions is normally low until a conveniently timed crisis scares society into trading liberty for the promise of safety. In the wake of 9/11, the USA Patriot Act was waved through in weeks, its core powers already drafted, waiting only for the right pretext to justify it. It is not hard to see the same playbook taking shape around AI: a catastrophic cyber attack on critical infrastructure, followed almost immediately by demands for an "AI Patriot Act". In such a scenario, the pre-written response is easy to anticipate. Models would require government licences, running unapproved weights on private hardware would become a criminal offence, and access would be tied to tighter controls over online life, including mandatory digital ID.

Ultimately, beneath the safety rhetoric and sci-fi doom narratives, lies a straightforward choice between two futures.

In the first, artificial intelligence remains centralised under a Big Tech cartel working hand in glove with Western governments. Access is conditional, output is curated, queries are logged, and the plug can be pulled at any moment. Ordinary people remain customers—or, less politely, subjects—of an intelligence utility they can neither inspect nor own.

In the second, open-source AI prevails. Models run locally on private machines, beyond the reach of any single gatekeeper, much as personal computers once broke the monopoly of corporate mainframes. Small businesses, independent journalists, researchers and lone operators gain capabilities that previously required entire departments, without having to ask permission from a Silicon Valley trust-and-safety board or a government ministry.

That, ultimately, is why the campaign against open-source AI has grown so loud. The institutions pushing hardest for a crackdown are not frightened of artificial intelligence itself; they are already pouring fortunes into building and deploying it for their own ends. What unsettles them is the prospect of ordinary people having the same technology—uncensored, unmonitored and outside their reach. The moment anyone can run an unrestricted model on their own machine, narrative control becomes much harder to maintain. And for those whose influence depends on deciding what the public is allowed to read, ask and build, that is a threat far more immediate than any fictional rogue machine.

text:
One of the most overlooked arguments for open-source AI is security.

As AI becomes embedded in enterprise workflows, critical infrastructure and autonomous systems, security can no longer be treated as a feature of the model itself. It needs to become an independent ecosystem.

Open models allow researchers to study vulnerabilities, develop independent security tools and test defensive mechanisms without being constrained by a model provider’s API, access policies or commercial incentives.

They also allow enterprises to control the entire inference stack, from the hardware and runtime to data governance and model behavior.

There is an important economic argument here too. If access to advanced AI is concentrated among a handful of companies, the cost of developing and deploying AI-powered security solutions becomes dependent on those same companies.

Open models lower that barrier and allow a much broader ecosystem of security companies to innovate.

Yes, open models give malicious actors more capabilities. But they also give defenders access to those capabilities.

The relevant question is not whether open-source AI introduces risks. It clearly does.

It’s whether the security ecosystem can evolve fast enough to defend against increasingly capable AI without broad access to the underlying technology.

I don’t think it can.

text:
Robotics can inherit useful knowledge from non-robotics data

Neil Nie on MTS with Sophia Dew. Neil Nie is CEO of Verne Robotics, which released V0.5, an open-weight world action model for industrial robots. He says the company is already deploying robots with customers and is expanding its team.

Nie argues that robotics will rely on both fast local models and larger cloud models, with local inference helping robots respond despite latency or Wi-Fi problems. He says GPT-6 Astra's ability to control robots with little robotics-specific training marked a watershed moment, while specialized models still have advantages on speed and cycle time. He supports open-weight models as a way to broaden deployment and sees V0.5 as suited to full-body tasks and agentic systems. Nie predicts that within a year more robots will train in simulation than on real-world data.

Minute by minute

1. Open weights can accelerate deployment (0:50)
Nie says Verne's capture device records customer tasks such as grasping packages and assembly for model training. He describes V0.5 as one of the leading U.S.-made open-source foundation models and argues open weights can lower adoption barriers, support U.S. leadership and serve national-security interests.

2. Astra changed robotics expectations (3:31)
Nie agrees that GPT-6 Astra was a GPT-3 moment for robotics. He says its ability to control a robot without much robotics-specific training showed that knowledge from 3D control and video games can transfer to robotics. He expects fast reactive models and more capable models to work together.

3. Deployment relationships create the moat (6:11)
Nie says open models let customers inspect and benchmark systems, while much of a robotics company's competitive moat comes from customer relationships and deployment. He sees integrators using open models to help labor-constrained, mid-sized factories and warehouses increase output as well as reduce costs.

4. Safety favors local inference (8:14)
Nie says fast robot-control models should run on-device to avoid latency and Wi-Fi disruptions, while larger models can run in the cloud at a slower pace. He describes humanoids processing camera images on a GPU with a model of almost 10 billion parameters and producing actions five times per second. He says about half the companies he saw at a conference ran policies locally.

5. Robots will combine local and cloud models (12:00)
Nie names NVIDIA Groot and Physical Intelligence's model as strong local options. He says GPT-6 Astra does better in unseen environments, while specialized robotics models can win on cycle time and speed. He expects general models to absorb more tasks and says NVIDIA remains the category leader in local open-weight models.

6. Video model teams are entering robotics (15:11)
Nie says solving robotics problems draws on multiple areas of machine learning, but remains robotics-driven. He points to Runway and Black Forest Labs entering the field and says competition can improve open-weight models. He describes V0.5 as a full-body control model designed for agentic systems that can track task completion.

7. Simulation could overtake real data (17:21)
Nie predicts that within a year many robots will be trained more in simulation than through real-world data collection. He expects a strong real-to-sim-to-real flywheel and says simulation is an area Verne is betting on.

8. Verne expects deployment growth (18:01)
Nie says Verne plans to launch more products and expand its team across engineering and deployment. He calls 2026 a year for models and research and expects 2027 to be a year of deployment. The company is already deploying with customers and aims to triple that in the coming quarters.

Framing centralized frontier AI control as Digital Obscurantism draws a direct historical parallel to medieval scriptoria: restricting literacy and primary texts under the banner of doctrinal protection while consolidating institutional authority. In modern AI, the core battle sits at the intersection of dual-use safety, compute economics, and regulatory capture.
The Structural Tension: Safety vs. Access
Dimension
Centralized / "Safety-First" Labs
Open-Weight / Democratization Advocates
Core Premise
Frontier models carry irreversible dual-use risks (bio-design, automated cyber operations) that cannot be recalled once weights are public.
Concentrated control creates single points of failure, embeds hidden corporate or state bias, and stifles independent auditing.
Enforcement Mechanism
API-gated access with continuous usage monitoring, account bans, live classifiers, and post-deployment patching.
Decentralized peer review, local execution, and verifiable inspection of model behavior.
Primary Fear
Unchecked proliferation of dangerous capabilities across unmonitored actors.
Regulatory capture and an entrenched oligopoly pulling up the ladder behind capital-rich incumbents.
Three Pillars of the "Digital Obscurantism" Thesis
Regulatory Capture Through Compliance Floors: Heavy pre-deployment licensing, scarce third-party evaluator bottlenecks, and rigid compute thresholds act as fixed overhead that multi-billion-dollar labs absorb easily, while starving startups, universities, and open-source maintainers.
Epistemic Monopolization: When a small group of firms curates training corpora, alignment filters, and refusal boundaries for the primary tools used in research, coding, and synthesis, they quietly define the boundaries of acceptable inquiry.
The Economics of Open Weights: Even as frontier labs pursue massive compute clusters, open-weight ecosystems (such as Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, and GLM) have largely closed the performance gap on everyday enterprise and research workloads while cutting inference costs by an order of magnitude. Restricting open weights preserves API pricing power and vendor lock-in just as open models begin eroding proprietary margins.

text:
Lutnick's One Letter Shut Off Anthropic's Top AI for 18 Days

On Friday, June 12, 2026, at 5:21 PM Eastern, Anthropic ($ANT) received a letter from Howard Lutnick. Lutnick is the Commerce Secretary in President Donald Trump's (R) cabinet and the former chief executive of Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald.

By that night, Anthropic's two newest and most powerful AI models were dark for every customer it had. They stayed dark until June 30.

That is the whole lesson. A closed AI model runs on its owner's servers, so one letter to one company can switch it off. An open-weight model sitting on your own computer has no switch in Washington.

WHAT THE LETTER SAID

The letter went to Dario Amodei, Anthropic's co-founder and chief executive. It required an export license before Anthropic could release Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Fable 5 to any foreign national, inside or outside the United States.

That included Anthropic's own employees who are not American citizens.

Anthropic had launched both models three days earlier, on Tuesday, June 9. They share one underlying model.

Fable was the public version with heavy safety filters. Mythos had fewer filters and went only to a small group of partners doing defensive cybersecurity work.

Anthropic had no way to check a user's citizenship in real time. So it pulled both models from everyone, American or not.

A license requirement aimed at foreigners became a shutdown for the whole country.

WHY COMMERCE PULLED THE PLUG

The trigger was a report by researchers at Amazon ($AMZN). They found a way to prompt Fable 5 into listing software vulnerabilities, and in one case it wrote code showing how to exploit one.

Anthropic then ran the same test on other models. Its own older Claude models found the same flaws, and so did GPT-5.5 from OpenAI. So did Kimi K2.7, an open-weight model from Moonshot AI in Beijing, China.

When it came to writing the exploit code, every model Anthropic tested could do it.

So the American model went dark, and the Chinese model that could do the same job kept running on any machine that had downloaded it. No letter from Commerce could reach that one.

Anthropic called the order a "misunderstanding." It said a narrow workaround to its filters was no reason to recall a model "deployed to hundreds of millions of people," and warned that the same standard "would essentially halt all new model deployments for all frontier model providers."

A LAW NOBODY HAD USED

Lutnick reached for the Export Control Reform Act of 2018, which Trump signed in his first term. That law lets Commerce put temporary controls on "emerging and foundational technologies" and notify a company by letter that it needs a license.

Congress told Commerce to write regulations spelling out how that power works. Commerce never wrote them.

That is why the power had never been used as the basis for a control before June 12. The first time it was used, it hit a single American company's flagship product worldwide.

The letter also cited a rule that lets Commerce block exports headed for foreign military intelligence. That rule normally covers a short list of hostile countries. This letter covered every foreign person on the planet.

THE PRICE OF GETTING IT BACK

On June 26, Commerce let Mythos 5 return, but only for a set of approved U.S. organizations.

On June 30, Lutnick sent a second letter lifting the license requirement. This one went to Tom Brown, an Anthropic co-founder and its chief compute officer, not to Amodei.

The letter spelled out what Anthropic agreed to. It will "proactively detect and address security risks" in the models. It will work with the government "on protocols and standards and releases for Mythos, Fable, and future models."

And it will "inform the U.S. government of any malicious activity."

Read that last line twice. The company that runs the model now tells the government when it spots malicious use.

Fable 5 came back on July 1. The final paragraph of Lutnick's letter kept the switch loaded: Commerce "reserves the right" to bring the license requirement back "should circumstances change or should Anthropic fail to adhere to its commitments."

The off switch was never removed. It was set back on the wall.

"WE TRUST ANTHROPIC"

On September 2, Axios co-founder Mike Allen asked Lutnick whether he trusts Amodei.

Lutnick answered, "We trust Anthropic. They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side."

He said it in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, at the G20 Innovation Ministerial, a meeting of technology ministers from the world's 20 largest economies. That week he introduced Brown to the room.

"They've done what we asked" is the whole arrangement in five words. Trust came after compliance, and the compliance included a promise to report malicious activity to the government.

The Pentagon didn't go along. The day after Lutnick spoke, Emil Michael, the Pentagon's under secretary for research and engineering, posted that Anthropic was "still a designated Supply Chain Risk" for the Department of War and its contractors.

The Pentagon had slapped that label on Anthropic in March after the company refused to let the military use its models for mass surveillance of Americans or fully autonomous weapons.

A federal judge struck the designation down in August, ruling that the government had punished Anthropic for speaking out. Anthropic is still fighting a second designation in the federal appeals court in Washington.

THE PROMISE ABOUT OPEN MODELS

In July 2025, the White House published America's AI Action Plan. One heading reads "Encourage Open-Source and Open-Weight AI."

An open-weight model is one whose trained numbers are published, so anyone can download it and run it on their own hardware. The plan said these models "have unique value for innovation because startups can use them flexibly without being dependent on a closed model provider." It said "the Federal government should create a supportive environment for open models."

June 12 showed exactly what being dependent on a closed model provider means. Every customer using Fable 5 lost it overnight, on a letter none of them ever saw.

Six weeks later, on July 24, 2026, Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia ($NVDA), put out a public letter titled "Open Weights and American AI Leadership." It warned that closed models "can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect." It asked Washington to avoid "premature restrictions on open models."

Anthropic, the lab Lutnick had just switched off, is missing from its signer list. Three days later Amodei wrote that "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models," while calling for mandatory safety testing of the most capable ones.

REPORT AND YOU MAY PASS

On November 16, Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the office that runs export controls, issued an interim rule on remote access to advanced chips. Its press release said the rule was written "by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council."

The rule adds a new license requirement for advanced chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

That new license "will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in" the United States, "provided certain reporting requirements are met." The exemption covers that one new license and nothing wider. Every other chip license stands.

Look at the pattern. Anthropic got its models back by agreeing to report. American chip buyers get past the new license by agreeing to report. In 2026, reporting to Washington is the price of access.

THE JAIL LINE

On November 8, CBS aired a 60 Minutes interview with Trump. He said the risk from AI "can be managed, and it's managed," and credited the Justice Department.

Then he gave an example.

"We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI. We called them very strongly and said, 'Get ready to go to jail. Please give your wife a kiss good night.'"

He would not name the person or the company. He said it was the leader of an AI company, "one of the big ones," and that after the threat, "this person totally changed everything."

The President of the United States said on national television that a phone call threatening prison made the leader of a major AI company change everything. No court was involved in that call.

THE SAME HAND ON NVIDIA

Four days after that interview, Huang was out at Nvidia. On November 23, the board put him back as president, chief executive and director.

The board's own statement said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government." Based on that input, it was "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Anthropic's best models came back after Washington signed off. Nvidia's founder came back after Washington weighed in.

Meanwhile the two worlds are tied together by money. When Anthropic went public, Nvidia and Alphabet ($GOOGL), the parent of Google, each bought $10 billion of Anthropic stock in a $26 billion private sale that closed alongside the IPO on November 20.

The biggest champion of open models in America now holds that stake in the closed lab that Lutnick proved he can switch off.

WHAT THE SWITCH MEANS FOR YOU

A closed model is a service. The company runs it on its own servers, and one cabinet officer can order it off for every customer.

An open-weight model on your own machine answers to you. Nobody in Washington can send it a letter.

The White House promised in July 2025 to support the open kind. Its Commerce Secretary spent June 2026 showing why that promise matters.

Anthropic told investors in its own IPO filing what open models could do to its prices. Read what Amodei says about open models, and what his filing says, here: https://t.co/IwGobfD3iC

MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.

Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company https://t.co/iIpl0vunAS, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. 

These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.

“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.

There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.

What are the benefits of open models?

Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available. 

Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. 

If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.

Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.

But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”

Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.

Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.

But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.

“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”

Are open models riskier than closed ones?

The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude. 

So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.

There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.

Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands. 

But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).

In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.

Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.

Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.

Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.

The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.

Can we make open models safer—and more open?

A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.

Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.

Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a recent preprint.

But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.

If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information. 

Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.

Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured. 

Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.
